headline: Toll from munitions blast near Kyiv reaches 38 as Ukraine orders an audit of arms stores
dek: A Russian strike on Friday evening set off a store of explosives beside houses in the village of Myla. Ukraine's own prosecutors and defence ministry are now examining why it was there.
summary: At least 38 people died after a Russian strike detonated a munitions store beside homes near Kyiv, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy; Ukrainian prosecutors have opened a negligence inquiry.

queries: empty country road at dawn fields
image.alt: A plain corrugated-metal storage building standing in open farmland under a grey sky, with no people in view

body.text: The number of people known to have died after explosions at a munitions store in the village of Myla, in the Bucha district west of Kyiv, reached 38 on Sunday. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave the figure on Telegram, saying 20 people were injured and four were still unaccounted for. Ukrainian officials have said throughout that the count is not final.

The Kyiv Post reported that a Russian strike hit the site at about 8.10pm local time on Friday, near the Kyiv-Chop highway. What killed most of the victims was not the strike itself but what followed: the warehouse held explosives, they detonated, and fire spread into the houses around it. About 50 residential buildings were damaged. The Ukrainian Air Force said the country was hit by at least two missiles and 267 drones over that night.
A count that has moved, and figures that do not agree

Every casualty number in this story is provisional, and they have not been reconciled. On Saturday morning the head of the Kyiv regional administration, Tymur Tkachenko, put the toll at 27 and said it might not be final. By Saturday afternoon Ukrainian officials had raised it to at least 37, and Mr Zelenskyy's Sunday statement raised it again to 38.
27 people are known to have died. And this figure may not be final.
body.cite: Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv regional administration, on Saturday, via Al Jazeera

body.text: The injured count is the clearest example of the problem. The Kyiv Post, citing Mr Tkachenko, reported 42 injured including four children, with seven taken to hospital, and 381 people evacuated including 59 children. Ukraine's defence ministry, in a statement carried by the Ukrainian agency UNN on Saturday afternoon, gave 37 dead and 15 injured. Mr Zelenskyy's Sunday post gave 20 injured. None of the sources consulted explains the differences, which may reflect different counting points, different definitions of injury, or people discharged. Readers should treat all three as unsettled.

The Associated Press reported that 34 of the dead were residents of a care facility for older people and people with disabilities, attributing that to Mr Tkachenko as relayed by Ukrainian media. RFE/RL separately reported that a nursing home was destroyed. That accounting has not been confirmed by an independent inquiry. This wire is not naming any of the dead or injured, though Ukrainian outlets have reported that the head of one local community council was among them, having gone to the scene as a first responder.

The unusual part of this story is that the inquiry now running is a Ukrainian one into Ukrainian decisions. The prosecutor's office has opened a criminal negligence investigation into whether it was lawful to store explosive material that close to housing, and into what permits and approvals the operating company held, Al Jazeera reported. Mr Zelenskyy confirmed the investigation and said the facts had to be established in full.
A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people.
body.cite: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, President of Ukraine, via RFE/RL

body.text: Ukraine's prime minister, Serhiy Koretskyi, said that making the same mistakes in the fifth year of a full-scale invasion is criminal negligence, in remarks carried by the Kyiv Post. Separately, the defence ministry ordered what UNN reported as a full audit of sites where weapons and ammunition are stored, stating that such facilities must not be located near residential buildings. No individual or company has been named or charged. RFE/RL noted a comparable detonation in July at Vyshneve, where a strike killed nine people and damaged more than 280 houses. Russia's defence ministry said the warehouse held components and launch boosters for long-range drones, according to the Associated Press. Ukrainian officials describe it as a store of shells, mines, ammunition and drones. Neither account has been independently verified. The difference bears on whether the site was a legitimate military target, a question none of the sources consulted has settled.
Moscow signals strikes on the power system

On Sunday Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram that its forces had begun preparing large-scale strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, presenting this as a response to Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and on fuel and energy facilities. The statement was reported by Euronews and the Associated Press. Ukraine has spent recent weeks striking Russian oil refineries and logistics targets on the argument that they fund the war, and the Associated Press reported that those strikes have caused significant fuel supply problems inside Russia — an assessment drawn from reporting rather than from published Russian data. An announced intention is not an attack: at the time of writing no such campaign had been reported as having begun.

body.title: What is provisional here
items: The death and injury figures come from Ukrainian officials and are described by them as liable to change.
Three different injured counts are in circulation, from 15 to 42.
Russia's description of the site and Ukraine's description of it differ, and neither is independently verified.
The threatened strikes on Ukraine's energy grid are, so far, a stated intention.

uncertain: The death toll is provisional. It moved from 27 to 37 to 38 over roughly 36 hours and Ukrainian officials say it may rise; four people were listed as unaccounted for on Sunday.

The injured count is unreconciled across three official sources: 42 (Kyiv regional administration, via the Kyiv Post), 15 (Ukraine's defence ministry, via UNN) and 20 (President Zelenskyy, Sunday). The sources consulted do not explain the differences.
The report that 34 of the dead were residents of a care facility comes from the Kyiv regional administration via Ukrainian media and has not been independently confirmed.

What the warehouse actually contained is contested. Ukrainian officials call it an ammunition store; Russia's defence ministry calls it a store of drone components and launch boosters. Neither account has been verified independently.

Sources also differ on timing: the Kyiv Post and RFE/RL place the strike on Friday evening, 28 August, while a Euronews report describes the attack as occurring from Saturday into early Sunday. The Friday evening timing is the account given by the Ukrainian outlet closest to the scene.
Who authorised the storage of explosives at the site, and under what permits, is the subject of the prosecutor's inquiry and is not established. No one has been charged.
It has not been established how many deaths were caused by the initial strike and how many by the secondary detonations and fire.
Whether Russia carries out the strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure that its defence ministry says it is preparing is not known.
Quotations from Ukrainian officials appear in slightly different English wordings across outlets because they are translations; each is reproduced here as it appeared in the outlet credited.
